Athletics.current_status: Funding for athletic complex improvements has been clarified as a separate issue from the upcoming June 10th budget vote and will be addressed at a later date. This follows a recent push for a synthetic surface at the stadium complex.
Athletics.overview:
On April 30, 2025, it was clarified that funding for athletic complex improvements is not part of the upcoming June 10th budget vote and will be addressed separately at a later date. This clarification follows a presentation on January 8, 2025, where Athletics Director Todd Livingston advocated for a synthetic surface at the stadium complex. He presented data indicating that 78% of student-athletes utilize the facility and argued that a synthetic surface would significantly increase playable hours, reduce cancellations, and allow more teams, such as field hockey, to practice and compete on campus.

Earlier, on March 25, 2024, the Athletics Director provided a comprehensive overview of the department, detailing its 25 high school and 18 middle school programs. He highlighted student participation rates, which are in the mid-40% range at the high school level, numerous coaching and student awards, and a new partnership with Huddle for live-streaming and game analysis. Shortly after this overview, on March 28, 2024, a Board member raised concerns regarding equity and accessibility in athletics, specifically questioning admission fees for events and policies requiring students to purchase their own essential gear, such as swimsuits, which could create barriers to participation for some families.

On June 10, 2024, the board recognized various student achievements, including a special acknowledgment of the Boys Outdoor Track and Field team for winning the state championship.

perspectives.Board: On March 28, 2024, a Board member raised concerns about equity and accessibility in athletics, specifically questioning admission fees for events and policies requiring students to purchase essential gear, which could create barriers to participation for some families.
perspectives.Administration: On January 8, 2025, Athletics Director Todd Livingston presented data supporting the installation of a synthetic surface at the stadium complex, arguing it would increase playable hours and reduce cancellations. On March 25, 2024, the Athletics Director also provided an overview of the department's programs, participation rates, awards, and a new partnership with Huddle.

Equity.current_status: The SPSD Board unanimously approved a new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026, which includes a crucial data collection component. This policy aims to understand and address systemic issues, following extensive discussions on equity and school reconfiguration.
Equity.overview:
The SPSD Board unanimously approved a new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026, after a teacher from the district's equity committee emphasized the crucial role of its data collection component in addressing systemic issues. This approval follows a period of significant debate and action regarding equity within the district, including the unanimous approval of the consent agenda and the agenda policy (BEDB) on the same date.

Prior to this, on April 29, 2026, the board deliberated a resolution to delay elementary school reconfiguration until the 2027-28 school year. This discussion highlighted a central tension between stakeholders prioritizing equity, often Kaler and Skillin staff, and those prioritizing neighborhood schools and walkability, such as Brown, Small, and Dyer families. This debate stemmed from earlier findings presented on October 15, 2024, which revealed stark demographic disparities between elementary schools like Skillin and Small, attributed to attendance zones. Board members had previously expressed frustration over the slow pace of addressing these long-known inequities, while others defended the decision to hire a consultant for a thoughtful solution. The board had also debated revisiting elementary school reconfiguration as a cost-saving measure on December 17, 2025, acknowledging the complex equity issues of racial segregation.

The district's commitment to equity has been a recurring theme, particularly following the resignation of DEI Director Mohammad Albi Hadley due to a racist email on January 22, 2024. The Superintendent pledged to continue diversity, equity, and inclusion work with urgency, leading to the hiring of Or Men Gildo Paolo as Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion on May 30, 2024. Efforts have included the formation of an internal equity team, staff affinity groups, and the development of a protocol for responding to harmful language, as updated on March 11, 2024. Concerns about equity have also extended to athletics, with discussions on March 28, 2024, regarding admission fees and essential gear costs creating barriers to participation. Furthermore, on January 12, 2026, the district reaffirmed its commitment to safety for all students in response to ICE activity, with calls for accelerated staff training and clearer public guidance to support vulnerable families.

perspectives.Board: Board members unanimously approved the new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026. On April 29, 2026, they expressed conflicting emotions while deliberating a delay in elementary school reconfiguration, weighing requests for more planning time against the urgency of addressing equity and promises made to the Kaler community. On January 12, 2026, they expressed significant concern over ICE activity. On December 17, 2025, members debated revisiting elementary school reconfiguration as a cost-saving measure, acknowledging complex equity issues of racial segregation. On October 15, 2024, some members expressed frustration over the slow pace of addressing long-known inequities, while others defended hiring a consultant. On April 8, 2024, they debated the committee's findings, grappling with the tension between maintaining neighborhood schools and creating integrated learning environments, with members like DeAngelo cautioning against busing and Shen and Holman advocating for disrupting the status quo. On March 28, 2024, a board member raised concerns about equity and accessibility in athletics.
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent reaffirmed the district's commitment to safety for all students on January 12, 2026. On October 15, 2024, the Superintendent presented data showing enrollment decline and stark demographic disparities between elementary schools. On May 30, 2024, the administration presented Or Men Gildo Paolo as the new Director of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion. On March 28, 2024, the administration responded to concerns about athletics equity, committing to investigate policies and remove financial barriers. On March 11, 2024, the Assistant Superintendent announced the search for a new DEI Coordinator and updated on the DEI action plan, including the formation of an internal equity team and staff affinity groups. On January 22, 2024, the Superintendent publicly addressed the racist email leading to Mohammad Albi Hadley's resignation, condemning the act and pledging continued DEI work.
perspectives.Staff: A teacher from the district's equity committee spoke in strong support of the new Educational Equity Policy on June 8, 2026, emphasizing the crucial role of its data collection component. On April 29, 2026, principals presented findings from community listening sessions where Kaler and Skillin staff often prioritized equity in the reconfiguration debate. Some teachers also urged the board to proceed immediately with reconfiguration, arguing a delay perpetuates inequity. On February 12, 2024, the Administrators' Association read a statement in solidarity with Mohammed Abbi Hadley, renewing their commitment to DEI work.
perspectives.Citizens: Public comment on April 29, 2026, revealed a deeply divided community regarding elementary school reconfiguration, with some parents and teachers urging immediate action and others advocating for delay due to concerns about neighborhood schools. Brown, Small, and Dyer families often prioritized neighborhood schools and walkability in reconfiguration feedback. On January 12, 2026, there were public calls for accelerated staff training and clearer public guidance to support vulnerable families. On February 12, 2024, citizens connected Mohammad Abbi Hadley's departure to broader equity issues, stressing that shuffling numbers is not enough and emphasizing the critical need to recruit and retain diverse staff. Student representatives on April 8, 2024, shared that their experiences in less diverse elementary schools left them unprepared for the diversity of middle and high schools, and on February 12, 2024, emphasized the need to recruit and retain diverse staff. A community leader was quoted on April 8, 2024, stating that 'busing brown and black kids puts added strain on families'.

FY2025 Budget.current_status: The district is currently facing a projected FY2025 budget deficit of $1.3 to $1.9 million, primarily due to newly ratified teacher and staff contracts. An immediate non-personnel spending freeze has been implemented for the remainder of the school year to curtail discretionary spending.
FY2025 Budget.overview:
The SPSD is currently grappling with a projected FY2025 budget deficit, estimated to be between $1.3 and $1.9 million, as reported by the Finance Committee on December 8, 2025. This deficit is primarily attributed to the financial impact of recently ratified teacher and staff contracts. In response, the district has initiated an immediate non-personnel spending freeze for the remainder of the school year to curb discretionary expenditures on supplies and services.

The FY2025 budget was successfully passed by South Portland voters with a significant 22% margin of support on June 18, 2025, following a referendum held on June 10, 2025 (May 12, 2025). Prior to the referendum, the budget process was complicated by a last-minute, higher-than-expected health insurance rate increase of 7.5%, which added an unforeseen $200,000 deficit to the proposed budget (March 24, 2025). This led to the Superintendent's final proposed budget being approximately $73 million with a 5.98% operating increase, a significant increase from the $69.28 million FY2025 school budget that the board had unanimously approved on May 13, 2024, to proceed to a city-wide referendum.

Earlier in the budget cycle, the administration presented revisions on April 8, 2024, which utilized savings from lower-than-expected health insurance costs, resulting in a proposed 4.88% increase over the previous year and including key additions such as a new district-level position for Mental Health and Student Intervention, additional stipends, and funds for security upgrades. These revisions followed initial proposals by the Superintendent in March 2024, which ranged from $69.4 million to $69.5 million, representing a 5% operating increase and a 3.8-3.82% school tax rate increase. The Superintendent emphasized the difficulty of the budget cycle due to rising fixed costs and the loss of $1.5 million in federal COVID-era funds that supported 19 positions (March 11, 2024; March 18, 2024; March 25, 2024; March 28, 2024). The Superintendent had previewed a difficult FY2025 budget season as early as February 12, 2024.

perspectives.Board: The board expressed a strong desire to keep the final tax impact at or below a 6% increase (March 24, 2025). They systematically voted on and unanimously approved the $69.28 million FY2025 school budget for referendum on May 13, 2024. Following the successful referendum, the board expressed gratitude to South Portland voters for passing the school budget (June 18, 2025).
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent consistently presented budget proposals, initially ranging from $69.4 million to $69.5 million with a 5% operating increase and a 3.8-3.82% school tax rate increase, emphasizing the challenges posed by rising fixed costs and the loss of federal COVID funds (March 2024). Revisions were made to achieve a 4.88% increase with new positions and security upgrades (April 8, 2024). The Superintendent's final proposed budget was approximately $73 million with a 5.98% operating increase, impacted by a last-minute health insurance rate hike (March 24, 2025). The Superintendent reminded the community about the upcoming referendum (May 12, 2025) and later expressed gratitude for its passage (June 18, 2025).
perspectives.Citizens: South Portland voters demonstrated strong support for the FY2025 school budget by passing the referendum with a significant 22% margin of support (June 18, 2025).

FY2026 Budget.current_status: Due to a district-wide spending freeze, the FY2026 budget is now projected to land closer to a small surplus or deficit, a significant improvement from earlier fears. The final financial outcome for the fiscal year remains uncertain, pending the official audit.
FY2026 Budget.overview:
On July 20, 2026, the Finance Director reported a positive shift in the FY2026 budget outlook. Thanks to a district-wide spending freeze, the budget is now projected to conclude closer to a small surplus or deficit, rather than the previously anticipated worst-case scenario. However, the final financial outcome for the fiscal year is still uncertain, awaiting the official audit. This update followed a November 3, 2025, report where the Finance Director projected a $337,000 deficit for FY2026, which was expected to be offset by a one-time $815,000 geothermal tax credit. At that time, a warning was issued regarding the district's nearing depletion of its fund balance, posing significant challenges for the subsequent FY2027 budget.

The FY2026 budget itself was formally approved on June 3, 2025, during a special meeting expedited to align with the City Council's schedule. At this meeting, the Superintendent presented 19 budget action items for the FY2026 school budget, totaling $73,131,556, which were subsequently voted on by the board. Leading up to this approval, the Superintendent had encouraged community members to vote in the June 10th school budget referendum for the 2025-2026 school year on April 30, 2025.

The initial budget proposal, presented by the Superintendent on March 10, 2025, outlined a 5.98% increase in the total school operating budget, amounting to $72.9 million, and requiring a $3.17 million increase from local taxpayers. This proposal was framed on April 7, 2025, as a necessary response to the district's lowest projected student enrollment in 15 years. Key drivers for a potential $9 million shortfall, as identified on March 10, 2025, included the loss of COVID-era and other carryover funds, contractual salary increases for three bargaining units, and rising health insurance costs. Earlier, on February 24, 2025, the Superintendent had highlighted a challenging FY2026 budget context, noting that a simple rollover of current services would necessitate an 11.4% local increase, and had already implemented a non-essential spending freeze with anticipated reductions in employee positions.

perspectives.Board: On June 3, 2025, the board voted to approve 19 budget action items for the FY2026 school budget, totaling $73,131,556, following a special meeting expedited for the City Council's schedule.
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent consistently presented the FY2026 budget, initially highlighting a challenging context on February 24, 2025, where a rollover of current services would require an 11.4% local increase, leading to a non-essential spending freeze and anticipated position reductions. On March 10, 2025, the Superintendent proposed a $72.9 million budget with a 5.98% increase, requiring $3.17 million from taxpayers, citing loss of COVID funds, contractual salary increases, and rising health insurance as key drivers. The Finance Director provided updates, noting on November 3, 2025, a projected $337,000 deficit for FY2026, offset by an $815,000 geothermal tax credit, while also warning of a nearing depletion of the fund balance impacting FY2027. Most recently, on July 20, 2026, the Finance Director reported that a district-wide spending freeze has improved the FY2026 budget projection to a small surplus/deficit, with the final outcome pending audit.

FY2027 Budget.current_status: The FY2027 budget was unanimously passed by the board on April 29, 2026, following the City Council's offer to forgive up to $2 million of the current year's deficit and guidance for a 6% tax impact. A resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline was also approved.
FY2027 Budget.overview:
On April 29, 2026, the board unanimously passed all articles of the FY2027 budget. This approval came after the Finance Director detailed the district's precarious financial state and the need for long-term stability, noting the City Council's generous offer to forgive up to $2 million of the current year's deficit and their guidance to maintain a 6% tax impact. In a separate but related vote, the board also approved, 5-1, a resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline, establishing a steering committee and committing to a final vote on the implementation plan by November 2026.

This successful passage followed an earlier rejection of the Superintendent's proposed FY2027 budget. On March 30, 2026, the board failed to pass the budget in a 2-5 vote, with members expressing concerns over specific personnel cuts (including DEI, special education, and arts), the rushed process, and a desire to first discuss funding options with the City Council. The administration had presented this budget on March 23, 2026, designed to address a significant financial crisis with a 6% local tax increase. On April 2, 2026, the Finance Director presented an updated FY27 budget, emphasizing a more realistic approach to expenses like electricity to avoid future deficits, given the district's lack of a savings buffer, while maintaining the 6.0% local tax increase guidance.

The budget development process began on December 17, 2025, with the board reviewing financial forecasts and providing initial guidance. The district faced a significant budget challenge for FY2027, with a projected $7.2 million gap due to declining enrollment, rising staffing, increased costs, and a depleted fund balance (February 4, 2026). Maintaining current services would have required an 18.95% tax increase, but the board set a target ceiling of 6%, necessitating $7-8 million in cuts (February 4, 2026; March 2, 2026). The administration's proposal on March 9, 2026, aimed to meet the City Council's 6% tax increase guidance, requiring approximately $8.4 million in reductions from the roll-forward budget. Public forums were announced on January 12, 2026, to gather input on cost-saving measures, with community desire for student-centered decisions and long-term fiscal stability noted on February 9, 2026.

perspectives.Board: On April 29, 2026, the board unanimously passed the FY2027 budget and, in a 5-1 vote, approved delaying the reconfiguration timeline. Earlier, on March 30, 2026, the board failed to pass the Superintendent's proposed budget (2-5 vote), with members citing concerns over specific personnel cuts (DEI, special education, arts), the rushed process, and the need to discuss funding with the City Council. The board had set a target ceiling of a 6% tax increase (February 4, 2026) and discussed the challenging budget on February 9, 2026. They also announced public forums on January 12, 2026, and provided initial guidance to the superintendent on December 17, 2025.
perspectives.Administration: The Finance Director detailed the district's precarious financial state and the need for long-term stability on April 29, 2026. She also presented the FY27 budget on April 2, 2026, highlighting a realistic approach to expenses and the lack of a savings buffer. The administration presented the Superintendent's Budget on March 23, 2026, designed to address a significant financial crisis with a 6% local tax increase. On March 9, 2026, they presented a proposal requiring $8.4 million in reductions to meet the 6% tax increase guidance. Dr. Johanna Prince led the presentation on February 4, 2026, detailing the $7.2 million budget gap and the need for significant cuts.
perspectives.Citizens: Public forums were announced on January 12, 2026, to gather input on creative cost-saving measures. Public forums revealed community desire for student-centered decisions and long-term fiscal stability (February 9, 2026).

Facilities.current_status: Remediation efforts are underway for the South Portland Middle School field, with a plan to make it playable by Fall 2026, though the district will not cover the costs. Security upgrades, including new surveillance cameras and secure vestibules, are being installed across elementary schools, with most projects completed or scheduled for completion by summer 2026.
Facilities.overview:
On January 12, 2026, an update was provided regarding the South Portland Middle School field, outlining a plan for aeration, overseeding, and fertilization in the spring to ensure playability by Fall 2026. The district explicitly stated it would not pay for this remediation. This follows a November 3, 2025 report from the Director of Operations detailing significant soil and turf issues at the field and a multi-step remediation plan, during which the board discussed holding the original contractor financially responsible. Major summer facilities projects were also underway as of July 14, 2025, including new surveillance camera systems and secure vestibules at all five elementary schools, alongside roofing work at Small, Kaler, and Skillin schools.

The implementation of security enhancements was further detailed on June 9, 2025, when the Director of Operations announced that security cameras would be installed in all five elementary schools over the summer. Additionally, new secure vestibules were scheduled for construction at Brown, Kaler, and Small elementary schools that summer, with Skillin and Dyer elementary schools slated for summer 2026. These projects align with updates provided on January 13, 2025, by the Buildings and Grounds Committee regarding the timeline for projects funded by recently passed school safety and maintenance bonds, which also noted ongoing HVAC issues at the middle school requiring significant staff time.

Regarding athletic facilities, on November 12, 2024, the administration decided to pause and research further before reintroducing the athletic complex proposal to the board, following the failure of its referendum. This decision came after the Board, on June 10, 2024, unanimously voted to direct the administration to prepare three separate bond referendum proposals—one for security, one for deferred maintenance, and one for athletic facilities—allowing for independent consideration, a modification from the administration's initial proposal for a single $17 million bond. The Superintendent had previewed these major facilities needs, including the high school stadium complex overhaul, during a workshop on May 13, 2024.

perspectives.Board: On November 3, 2025, the board discussed holding the original contractor financially responsible for the South Portland Middle School field remediation. On November 12, 2024, the board supported surveying families and students for input on moving high school graduation from the stadium to a larger venue. On June 10, 2024, the board unanimously voted to direct the administration to prepare three separate bond referendum proposals (security, deferred maintenance, athletic facilities) for independent consideration, rather than a single bond.
perspectives.Administration: On January 12, 2026, the district maintained it would not pay for the South Portland Middle School field remediation. On November 3, 2025, the Director of Operations reported on significant soil and turf issues at the South Portland Middle School field and outlined a remediation plan. On July 14, 2025, the Director of Operations reported on major summer facilities projects underway. On June 9, 2025, the Director of Operations announced security camera installations at all five elementary schools and secure vestibule construction at Brown, Kaler, and Small that summer, with Skillin and Dyer scheduled for summer 2026. On November 12, 2024, the administration decided to pause and research before bringing back the athletic complex proposal after its referendum failure. On June 10, 2024, the administration presented a potential bond referendum of up to $17 million to address major facility needs. On May 13, 2024, the Superintendent previewed an upcoming workshop on major facilities needs, including security upgrades, deferred maintenance, and the high school stadium complex overhaul.
perspectives.Citizens: On July 8, 2024, numerous citizens, including parents and youth sports coaches, spoke in strong support of all three referenda, especially the stadium project, emphasizing the current field's poor condition, the need for reliable and safe facilities, and the embarrassment of substandard facilities compared to neighboring towns.

Kaler Closure.current_status: The Kaler Elementary School closure is moving forward, with a parent survey recently distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for the upcoming school year. An elementary reconfiguration steering committee is also actively meeting.
Kaler Closure.overview: On May 11, 2026, an update was provided regarding the Kaler Elementary School closure, confirming that a parent survey had been distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for the upcoming school year. Additionally, the 23-member elementary reconfiguration steering committee's progress was noted, with its meetings confirmed to be open to the public.

perspectives.Citizens: A parent survey was distributed to gather input on student placement priorities for the upcoming school year following the Kaler Elementary School closure, indicating an effort to solicit public input on the transition.

Reconfiguration.current_status: The SPSD Board is currently engaged in workshops on elementary school reconfiguration, emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic and demographic imbalances between schools. A steering committee is actively working, and the board has committed to a final vote on an implementation plan by November 2026, following a decision to delay full reconfiguration until the 2027-28 school year.
Reconfiguration.overview:
On July 20, 2026, the board held the first of several workshops on elementary school reconfiguration, with board members providing initial guidance emphasizing the need to address socioeconomic and demographic imbalances between schools. This follows an update on May 11, 2026, regarding a 23-member elementary reconfiguration steering committee, whose meetings are open to the public, and a parent survey distributed for Kaler Elementary School student placement. Crucially, on April 29, 2026, the board, in a 5-1 vote, approved a resolution to delay the reconfiguration timeline until the 2027-28 school year, establishing the steering committee and committing to a final vote on the implementation plan by November 2026. This decision effectively reversed the board's earlier 4-2 vote on March 30, 2026, which had selected 'Option A' to reconfigure schools into a Primary (Pre-K to 1st) and Intermediate (2nd to 4th) model, effective for the 2026-2027 school year.

Prior to the delay, the board had been moving towards a 2026-2027 implementation. On April 2, 2026, the Chair clarified that the public budget vote was separate from the reconfiguration decision. The administration's rationale for reconfiguration, presented on March 2, 2026, included addressing declining enrollment, creating more equitable demographic balances, and increasing opportunities for teacher collaboration. This came after the board unanimously voted on February 9, 2026, to request a formal proposal from the superintendent on the benefits and impacts of reconfiguring elementary schools, stressing the need for data and community input. Earlier, on March 9, 2026, the administration presented a revised proposal to close Dyer Elementary School, keeping the remaining four schools in a Pre-K/K-4 configuration, as part of a budget reduction plan.

The discussion around reconfiguration has a longer history, with board members debating revisiting it as a cost-saving measure on December 17, 2025, acknowledging complex equity issues. On May 13, 2024, after a lengthy debate, the board approved a path forward including reviewing the Brick Hill neighborhood's school assignment, providing more resources to schools with higher economic disadvantage, creating a policy for regular attendance zone review, and hiring a consultant to analyze attendance zones, configurations, and controlled choice/magnet models, with findings due by January 2025. This followed recommendations from the Elementary Boundaries and Configuration Steering Committee on February 12, 2024, for short-term actions and long-term expert impact studies on grade-level reconfiguration, magnet programming, and controlled-choice models to create more integrated and equitable schools.

On April 29, 2026, members expressed conflicting emotions, weighing administration and staff requests for more planning time against the urgency of equity issues and promises to the Kaler community, ultimately voting 5-1 to delay reconfiguration until the 2027-28 school year. This reversed their March 30, 2026 decision, where they voted 4-2 to select 'Option A' for a 2026-2027 implementation, with proponents citing long-term equity and efficiency benefits. On February 9, 2026, the board unanimously voted to request a formal proposal on reconfiguration, stressing data and community input. On March 2, 2026, the administration presented nine detailed scenarios for reconfiguration, with the rationale to address declining enrollment, create more equitable demographic balances, and increase teacher collaboration. Some staff urged immediate reconfiguration, arguing delay perpetuates inequity and betrays the Kaler community. Others advocated for delay, citing the need for a more thorough process. On April 2, 2026, staff voiced strong opposition to the rushed reconfiguration timeline, citing lack of a detailed plan, inadequate community input, and concerns about impact on students, families, and morale. On March 30, 2026, staff voiced significant concerns about staff cuts, the rushed timeline, and perceived lack of transparency. On May 11, 2026, a parent survey was distributed regarding Kaler Elementary student placement. On April 29, 2026, public comment revealed a deeply divided community, with some parents urging immediate reconfiguration for equity and others advocating for delay due to concerns about neighborhood schools and the need for more evidence. Special Education.current_status: The district is currently navigating increased special education responsibilities due to new state mandates for pre-K services, while simultaneously facing budget cuts that eliminate two elementary occupational therapist positions, raising concerns about service delivery and legal compliance.
Special Education.overview:
On March 23, 2026, the district reported a special education population of 23% and discussed budget plans that include eliminating two elementary occupational therapist positions. These cuts raised concerns regarding student safety and the district's ability to meet legally mandated service requirements. This development follows the March 2, 2026 discussion where the district outlined plans for new state mandates, requiring it to assume responsibility for special education services for 4-year-olds in the next school year and 3-year-olds the year after, which will significantly increase the number of students served.

Prior to these discussions, on April 30, 2025, the Assistant Superintendent confirmed that the district was in a 'fact-finding' phase concerning the multi-year transition of pre-K special education services from Child Development Services (CDS) to the district, in response to a public question.

Further back, on March 25, 2024, the Director of Special Education presented a comprehensive overview of the department, which at that time served 649 students. The presentation detailed the types of disabilities addressed, the range of services provided, the Individualized Education Program (IEP) process, and emphasized the importance of delivering services in the least restrictive environment.

perspectives.Administration: The Assistant Superintendent indicated on April 30, 2025, that the district was in a 'fact-finding' phase regarding the pre-K special education transition. The Director of Special Education provided a detailed overview of the department's services on March 25, 2024. The administration is also planning for new state mandates to assume responsibility for pre-K special education services, as discussed on March 2, 2026.
perspectives.Citizens: Concerns were raised on March 23, 2026, regarding student safety and the district's ability to meet legally mandated service requirements due to the elimination of occupational therapist positions. A public question was also posed on April 30, 2025, regarding the pre-K special education transition.

Student Recognition.current_status: The SPSD Board consistently recognizes student achievements across academics, arts, and extracurriculars, with recent celebrations for top scholars, the marching band, and the robotics team. This ongoing practice highlights diverse student successes and provides direct acknowledgment from the board.
Student Recognition.overview:
On May 11, 2026, the board celebrated the South Portland High School Top Scholars for 2026. The ceremony involved students introducing their peers and detailing their academic achievements, extracurricular involvement, and future university and career plans. This recognition followed a similar event on November 3, 2025, where the board honored the South Portland High School marching band for winning a gold medal and a five-star rating at the Maine Band Directors Association state finals.

Earlier, on May 27, 2025, the SPHS Robotics Team 58, the Riot Crew, received recognition for their impressive performance at the World Championships in Houston, where they ranked in the top 3%. The team demonstrated their robot for the board and was presented with certificates. The district's commitment to student success was evident when, on March 24, 2025, the Superintendent announced the Robotics Team's qualification for the World Championships and pledged financial support to ensure their participation.

Further back, on March 10, 2025, the board celebrated the South Portland High School Girls' Basketball team for winning the state championship. During the same meeting, three SPHS students were also recognized for their Scholastic Art Awards, showcasing the board's broad approach to acknowledging student excellence in various fields.

perspectives.Board: The board consistently engages in direct recognition of student achievements across academics, arts, and athletics. They have celebrated top scholars, championship-winning sports teams, award-winning marching bands, and high-achieving robotics teams. The board also provided financial support for the Robotics Team's participation in the World Championships.
perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent announced the SPHS Robotics Team's qualification for the World Championships and confirmed the district's financial support to facilitate their attendance.

Superintendent Search.current_status: The SPSD Board has identified a preferred candidate for the superintendent position and has authorized contract negotiations. A public announcement will be made once negotiations are concluded.
Superintendent Search.overview:
On May 11, 2026, the board announced it had identified a preferred candidate for the superintendent position and unanimously voted to authorize the chair to enter into contract negotiations, with a public announcement pending conclusion. This followed the announcement on April 29, 2026, that two finalists had been selected, and a community meet-and-greet was scheduled for May 6th. The search process, guided by Zeal Education Group, involved confidential interviews conducted solely by the school board and its student representatives, as confirmed on March 9, 2026.

Earlier in the process, on February 9, 2026, the board approved a one-time exception allowing student representatives to participate in semi-finalist interviews under strict confidentiality rules, while Zeal Education Group facilitated community feedback through on-site meetings and a Thought Exchange survey. A board member made a direct appeal on February 4, 2026, for greater community participation, noting low attendance at virtual feedback sessions. The board formally approved a contract with Zeal Education Group on January 12, 2026, also allocating funds for national advertising and comprehensive background checks. Prior to this, on December 17, 2025, a public workshop with Zeal Education Group was announced for December 22nd, alongside a community forum for January 22nd, following a December 8, 2025, workshop where three firms presented their proposals.

The search for a new superintendent began on June 18, 2025, when the board voted to initiate a search for an interim superintendent and engage the Maine School Management Association (MSMA) for assistance. Concurrently, a motion was passed to authorize the board chair and legal counsel to negotiate a separation agreement with Superintendent Metheny, contingent upon a successful interim superintendent search. Board members at that time emphasized the importance of leadership stability, expressing openness to an interim superintendent serving for the entire school year to minimize transitions.

perspectives.Board: The Board has actively managed the superintendent search, from initiating the process and selecting search firms to identifying finalists and a preferred candidate. On June 18, 2025, they voted to initiate a search for an interim superintendent and engage MSMA, while also authorizing negotiations for a separation agreement with Superintendent Metheny. They formally approved a contract with Zeal Education Group on January 12, 2026, and later, on February 9, 2026, voted to allow student representatives to participate in semi-finalist interviews under strict confidentiality. A board member appealed for greater community participation on February 4, 2026, citing low attendance at feedback sessions. On May 11, 2026, the board unanimously voted to authorize the chair to enter into contract negotiations with a preferred candidate.
perspectives.Administration: Several administrators voiced strong disappointment on April 29, 2026, regarding the closed nature of the superintendent search process, arguing that the lack of stakeholder involvement and transparency contradicted the board's stated values and devalued the expertise of district employees.
perspectives.Staff: Union leaders from SPTA and SPESPA expressed strong disappointment on April 29, 2026, with the closed superintendent search process, stating that the lack of stakeholder involvement and transparency was contrary to the board's stated values and devalued the expertise of district employees.

Transportation.current_status: The district has committed to providing three buses for large track meets and engaged a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the upcoming school year to address overcrowding, particularly in the Brick Hill area.
Transportation.overview:
On June 8, 2026, the administration presented detailed plans to address recent transportation complaints. These plans included a commitment to providing three buses for large track meets and engaging a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the next school year. The goal of this re-optimization is to alleviate overcrowding, particularly in the Brick Hill area.

These administrative actions followed significant safety concerns raised on May 11, 2026. During public comment, parents and a transportation employee highlighted severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, with students reportedly sitting in aisles. In response to these concerns, the superintendent pledged to investigate the issue immediately.

perspectives.Administration: On May 11, 2026, the superintendent pledged to investigate significant bus overcrowding issues immediately. By June 8, 2026, the administration presented detailed plans, committing to providing three buses for large track meets and engaging a consultant to re-optimize all bus routes for the next school year to alleviate overcrowding, especially in the Brick Hill area.
perspectives.Staff: On May 11, 2026, a transportation employee raised significant safety concerns regarding severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, noting students sitting in aisles.
perspectives.Citizens: On May 11, 2026, parents raised significant safety concerns about severe overcrowding on buses for athletic events and regular morning routes, with reports of students sitting in aisles.

Adult Education.current_status: The Adult Education program is experiencing rapid growth, particularly in ESOL and new Integrated Education and Training (IET) programs. However, it faces a significant funding challenge due to its nearly 70% reliance on unstable grants, necessitating increased local investment for sustainability.
Adult Education.overview:
On December 9, 2024, the Director of Adult Education presented on the program's rapid growth, specifically mentioning ESOL services and the new Integrated Education and Training (IET) program. She highlighted a significant funding challenge, noting the program is nearly 70% reliant on unstable grants, and signaled a clear need for increased local investment in the upcoming budget to ensure the program's long-term sustainability.

This follows earlier reports of exponential growth. On March 25, 2024, the Director of Adult Education highlighted that the program had become the third largest in Maine. At that time, it was already noted as heavily reliant on grants, having expanded its ESOL classes to five levels and developing digital skills and job training programs to meet high community demand.

perspectives.Administration: The Administration, through the Director of Adult Education, has consistently reported rapid and exponential growth in the Adult Education program, particularly in ESOL and new IET/job training initiatives. They have identified a critical funding challenge, noting the program's nearly 70% reliance on unstable grants, and advocate for increased local investment to ensure its long-term sustainability.

Community School Model.current_status: The Community School model at South Portland Middle School has demonstrated success in reducing absenteeism and increasing family engagement, prompting a discussion about sustainable funding for its continuation and potential district-wide expansion.
Community School Model.overview:
On October 15, 2024, the board received a detailed presentation from the principal and community school director of South Portland Middle School concerning their successful Community School model. The presentation outlined the model's six core practices and showcased positive results, such as reduced chronic absenteeism and enhanced family engagement within the school community.

The presenters underscored the necessity of securing sustainable funding to not only maintain the current successful operations of the model but also to explore its potential for district-wide expansion. This highlights the board's upcoming challenge to consider financial strategies that would support the continuation and growth of this effective educational approach.

Snow Day Policy.current_status: The SPSD has implemented a new snow day policy, eliminating remote learning for the first five snow days and instead adding them to the end of the school year. This change was made due to concerns about remote learning's effectiveness for younger students.
Snow Day Policy.overview:
On November 12, 2024, the Administration announced a significant change to the snow day policy. This new policy eliminates remote learning days for the first five snow days, opting instead to add these days to the end of the school year. The Superintendent cited that remote learning days are not a good fit for the youngest learners as the primary reason for this modification.

The South Portland Teacher Association (SPTA) representatives voiced concerns regarding this policy shift during the November 12, 2024 meeting. They highlighted that staff had made plans based on the previously approved calendar and the established practice of utilizing remote days for inclement weather. The SPTA urged the board to engage in collaborative discussions with educators to develop a more equitable and effective plan for managing snow days.

perspectives.Administration: On November 12, 2024, the Superintendent announced the elimination of remote learning for the first five snow days, stating these days would instead be added to the end of the school year. This decision was based on the belief that remote learning is not effective for the youngest learners.
perspectives.Staff: During the November 12, 2024 meeting, the South Portland Teacher Association (SPTA) representatives expressed concern about the new snow day policy. They noted that staff had already made plans according to the prior calendar and the practice of remote learning days, advocating for collaboration with educators to create a more equitable and effective inclement weather plan.

Student Achievement.current_status: Roughly half of students meet grade-level benchmarks and 40% meet growth targets according to NWEA MAP data, while SAT scores are below state and national averages. The administration recognizes the need to focus on improving SAT scores to support students' post-secondary aspirations.
Student Achievement.overview: On January 22, 2024, the Superintendent presented NWEA MAP data indicating that approximately half of students are meeting grade-level benchmarks, and about 40% are achieving their growth targets. Concurrently, SAT scores were reported to be below both state and national averages. The administration acknowledged these SAT results as a critical area requiring focused attention to ensure students are adequately prepared to achieve their post-secondary goals.

perspectives.Administration: The Superintendent shared NWEA MAP data regarding student benchmarks and growth targets, and acknowledged that SAT scores, which are below state and national averages, are an area needing focus to ensure students can achieve their post-secondary goals.

Student Mental Health.current_status: The district is actively focusing on student mental health through family nights, virtual forums, and partnerships with organizations like NAMI and AFSP, following recent tragedies. New initiatives include universal screeners, a formal mental health action plan, and the recent hiring of a Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.
Student Mental Health.overview:
On October 15, 2024, the student representative reported on school activities, including a family night focused on mental health. The high school principal and superintendent further elaborated on this event and a separate virtual forum, highlighting the district's ongoing commitment to student mental health and its partnerships with organizations such as NAMI and the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.

Prior to this, on September 9, 2024, the Administration addressed the tragic suicides of three students, acknowledging the severity of the situation. The Superintendent detailed the existing mental health resources available and outlined significant future actions, which included the implementation of universal screeners, the development of a formal mental health action plan, and the welcoming of the district's first Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.

perspectives.Administration: On October 15, 2024, the high school principal and superintendent elaborated on district efforts, including family nights and virtual forums, and highlighted partnerships with NAMI and the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention. On September 9, 2024, the Superintendent addressed recent student suicides, detailed current resources, and outlined future actions such as universal screeners, a formal mental health action plan, and the hiring of a Director of Mental and Behavioral Health.

AI in Education.current_status: The SPSD Board is adopting 'Magic School AI' as a controlled tool, alongside developing staff competency training and a student curriculum for AI integration.
AI in Education.overview: On July 8, 2024, the Technology Director presented the AI Steering Committee's progress to the board. This included the adoption of "Magic School AI" as a controlled tool for the district, the development of comprehensive staff competency training programs, and the creation of a dedicated curriculum for students on AI. These initiatives aim to integrate AI responsibly into the educational environment.

perspectives.Board: During the July 8, 2024 meeting, the board engaged in discussions regarding the critical balance between leveraging AI's benefits and ensuring the preservation of essential student skills, such as writing.
perspectives.Administration: On July 8, 2024, the Technology Director, representing the AI Steering Committee, recommended and presented the adoption of 'Magic School AI' as a controlled tool, along with plans for staff training and student curriculum development.

District Goals.current_status: The district's 2024-2025 'Pillars and Priorities' have been presented, focusing on improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism, and expanding mental and behavioral health supports. These priorities align with the recently introduced 'Together We Grow' theme and four key pillars.
District Goals.overview:
On September 9, 2024, the Administration presented the district's four 'Pillars and Priorities' for the 2024-2025 school year. Key goals outlined include improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism by another 5%, and continuing to build out mental and behavioral health supports.

This presentation followed the Superintendent's introduction on August 19, 2024, of the 2024-25 district theme, "Together We Grow." During this meeting, four key pillars were outlined: Instructional Excellence, DEIB, Operational Effectiveness, and a new pillar for Strategic Planning, which will address future school configurations and boundaries.

perspectives.Administration: On August 19, 2024, the Superintendent introduced the 2024-25 district theme, "Together We Grow," and outlined four key pillars for the year. Subsequently, on September 9, 2024, the Administration presented the specific 'Pillars and Priorities' for the 2024-2025 school year, detailing goals such as improving student engagement, reducing chronic absenteeism by 5%, and enhancing mental and behavioral health supports.

K-4 Math Curriculum.current_status: The SPSD Board is currently considering the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for K-4, which would replace the long-standing 'Investigations' curriculum. A vote on this quarter-million-dollar adoption is scheduled for January.
K-4 Math Curriculum.overview: On December 9, 2024, the Director of Curriculum formally recommended the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for grades K-4. This new curriculum is proposed to replace the 'Investigations' curriculum, which has been in use for 20 years. The recommendation emerged from a thorough review process conducted by a committee of educators. During the meeting, the Board engaged in discussions regarding the implications of this transition for both teachers and families, with a particular focus on multilingual learners. The Board is slated to vote on this significant quarter-million-dollar adoption in January.

perspectives.Board: The Board discussed the practical aspects of transitioning to a new curriculum, specifically considering the impact on teachers and multilingual learners. They are scheduled to vote on the proposed adoption in January.
perspectives.Administration: The Director of Curriculum recommended the adoption of the 'Into Math' program for K-4, based on a thorough review process conducted by an educator committee, to replace the existing 20-year-old 'Investigations' curriculum.
perspectives.Staff: Educators participated in a committee that conducted a thorough review process, leading to the recommendation of the 'Into Math' program for K-4.

Mental & Behavioral Health.current_status: The new Director of Mental and Behavioral Health is prioritizing suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, and has applied for opioid settlement funds with SoPo Unite to expand services.
Mental & Behavioral Health.overview: On December 9, 2024, the new Director of Mental and Behavioral Health provided an update on the department's strategic focus. This includes a comprehensive approach to suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, a response prompted by recent community tragedies. The Director also highlighted ongoing partnerships with various national and local organizations and announced a grant application submitted in collaboration with SoPo Unite, seeking opioid settlement funds to further enhance mental health services within the district.

perspectives.Administration: The Director of Mental and Behavioral Health outlined the department's focus on suicide prevention, intervention, and postvention, citing recent community tragedies as a catalyst. She also detailed partnerships with various organizations and the submission of a grant application with SoPo Unite for opioid settlement funds to bolster mental health services.

School Climate.current_status: Panorama survey data indicates that while younger students feel safe, older students (grades 6-12) report a low sense of belonging, reinforcing the district's "You Belong Here" initiative.
School Climate.overview: On January 22, 2024, the district reviewed Panorama survey data concerning school climate. The findings highlighted that younger students generally feel safe within the school environment. However, a significant concern emerged regarding older students (grades 6-12), with only 41% reporting a favorable sense of belonging. This data is being used to reinforce the district's ongoing "You Belong Here" theme, aiming to improve the overall school climate, particularly for secondary students.

Service Employees Contract.current_status: The South Portland School District Board ratified a three-year contract (FY25-27) with the South Portland School District Service Employees Association (SPESPA) on November 12, 2024. This concludes the negotiation process.
Service Employees Contract.overview: On November 12, 2024, the board officially ratified the three-year contract covering fiscal years 2025-2027 with the South Portland School District Service Employees Association (SPESPA). Both the board's negotiating team and the superintendent commended the collaborative and professional approach taken during the negotiation process.

perspectives.Board: The board's negotiating team praised the collaborative and professional nature of the negotiations (November 12, 2024).
perspectives.Administration: The superintendent commended the collaborative and professional nature of the negotiations (November 12, 2024).

Student Data.current_status: Recent data from SPHS indicates positive trends, including a significant decrease in chronic absenteeism, a reduction in out-of-school suspensions, and a lower course failure rate.
Student Data.overview: On July 8, 2024, the SPHS Principal presented encouraging student data trends to the board. This data highlighted a notable decrease in chronic absenteeism, moving from 42.3% to 35.5%. Furthermore, out-of-school suspensions saw a substantial 66% reduction, and the course failure rate improved from 6.7% to 4.4%.

perspectives.Administration: The SPHS Principal shared positive data trends, demonstrating improvements in chronic absenteeism, out-of-school suspensions, and course failure rates.

Student Support Systems.current_status: The SPSD is actively implementing a Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) framework across elementary, middle, and high schools to identify and provide targeted interventions for struggling students.
Student Support Systems.overview: On March 18, 2024, principals from all school levels presented detailed information on the Multi-Tiered Systems of Support (MTSS) framework. They elucidated how this tiered approach is utilized for both academic and behavioral support, designed to identify students who are struggling and subsequently provide universal, targeted, and intensive interventions to ensure their success.

perspectives.Administration: Principals from elementary, middle, and high schools delivered comprehensive presentations on the MTSS framework, detailing its implementation and purpose in supporting student success through tiered interventions.

Student Enrollment.current_status: Declining student enrollment is a significant factor contributing to a projected $7.2 million budget gap for FY2027, necessitating substantial cuts to maintain the district's financial stability.
Student Enrollment.overview: On February 4, 2026, the Administration, led by Dr. Johanna Prince, presented a critical financial challenge for the upcoming FY2027 budget. A major contributing factor to a projected $7.2 million budget gap is declining student enrollment, alongside rising staffing levels, increased costs, and a depleted fund balance. This situation necessitates significant cuts to district services, as maintaining current services would require an 18.95% tax increase, far exceeding the board's target ceiling of 6%.

perspectives.Administration: The Administration, through Dr. Johanna Prince, identified declining student enrollment as a key driver of the projected $7.2 million budget deficit for FY2027, highlighting its impact on the district's financial health.

Board Governance.current_status: Concerns about board governance, particularly regarding public notice and transparency in decision-making, were raised at the most recent meeting. Board members acknowledged and apologized for recent procedural missteps.
Board Governance.overview:
The most recent development on June 8, 2026, saw significant concerns raised regarding board governance. Public commenters and board members themselves highlighted issues with the lack of public notice for a special meeting and the inclusion of an un-agendized compensation vote. This indicates a breakdown in established governance procedures and transparency.

On June 8, 2026, board members Feller, Richardson, and Holman publicly apologized for the rushed decision, acknowledging a failure to understand public sentiment during a period of austerity and a general breakdown in transparency. This suggests an internal recognition of the governance issues and a commitment to address them.

perspectives.Board: On June 8, 2026, several board members, including Feller, Richardson, and Holman, publicly apologized for a rushed decision, a failure to "read the room" during a time of austerity, and a breakdown in transparency related to an un-agendized compensation vote and lack of public notice for a special meeting. Other board members also raised serious concerns about board governance.
perspectives.Citizens: On June 8, 2026, public commenters raised serious concerns about board governance, specifically citing the lack of public notice for a special meeting and the addition of an un-agendized compensation vote.

Student Cell Phone Policy 2026.current_status: The SPSD Board recently approved the second read of a new state-mandated cell phone policy (JICI) requiring phones to be off and away bell-to-bell. Specific implementation procedures will be developed at the school level and reviewed by the board later.
Student Cell Phone Policy 2026.overview:
On July 20, 2026, the board approved the second read of a new state-mandated cell phone policy, designated as JICI. This policy mandates that student cell phones must be off and away for the duration of the school day, from bell to bell.

During the discussion on July 20, 2026, it was clarified that while the core policy itself is now established, the detailed procedures for its implementation will be developed at the individual school level. These school-specific implementation plans will subsequently be brought before the board for review at a later date.

perspectives.Board: On July 20, 2026, the board approved the second read of the state-mandated cell phone policy (JICI) and engaged in a lengthy discussion to clarify that implementation procedures would be developed at the school level and reviewed later.
perspectives.Administration: On July 20, 2026, the administration was involved in the discussion clarifying that school-level implementation procedures would be developed and later reviewed by the board, following the approval of the state-mandated policy.
